concepts.def: Visual ordering of information by size, weight, colour and placement so the viewer reads the most important content first.
Underlying structure organising layout into columns and rows, popularised by Swiss design in the 1950s.
Coherent visual system including logo, typography and colour palette communicating an organisation's character.
Unoccupied area around and between elements in a design, used actively by Saul Bass in his film posters.
Image defined by mathematical paths rather than pixels, allowing scaling without loss of quality, used in logos.
Four-colour subtractive printing process using cyan, magenta, yellow and black, standard for full-colour printed work.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Graphic Communication — a core area of GCSE Art & Design.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Graphic Communication brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Graphic Communication.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which designer is famed for using negative space in mid-twentieth-century film posters?
Which colour model is standard for full-colour print production?

numericals.q: How many ink colours does CMYK printing use?

free_texts.q: What is the underlying column-based layout structure called?
